items.stem: A company stores sensitive files in an Amazon S3 bucket that uses server-side encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key (SSE-KMS). The key policy allows IAM policies in the account to control access to the key. A new application role has an IAM policy that allows s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on the bucket and allows no KMS actions. The application only downloads existing objects from the bucket. Every request from the application fails with an access denied error. Which change will fix the problem with LEAST privilege?
keywords: only downloads existing objects from the bucket

options.text: Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the customer managed key that encrypts the bucket.
options.why: A download of an SSE-KMS object needs [kms:Decrypt permissions for the key](../facts/kms.md#kms-s3-sse-kms-put-get-permissions), and this statement adds that one action on that one key.

options.text: Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:GenerateDataKey on the ARN of the customer managed key that encrypts the bucket.
options.why: The application downloads objects. An upload needs [kms:GenerateDataKey permissions on the key](../facts/kms.md#kms-s3-sse-kms-put-get-permissions), but a download needs kms:Decrypt, which this statement leaves out.
options.misconception: uses the permission that S3 needs for uploads to fix a failed download

options.text: Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows every KMS action, kms:*, on every KMS key in the account.
options.why: It works, but it allows every KMS action on every key, and least privilege gives principals [only the permissions they need](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-least-privilege-key-arns).
options.misconception: fixes one missing action by allowing every action on every key

options.text: Replace the S3 statements in the IAM policy of the role with one statement that allows every Amazon S3 action, s3:*, on the bucket.
options.why: S3 actions do not open the KMS key: no principal, [including the account root user or key creator](../facts/kms.md#kms-no-principal-has-access-unless-allowed), can use a key without an explicit allow.

items.explanation: SSE-KMS puts a KMS key between the role and the data. To download an object, the caller needs [kms:Decrypt permissions for the key](../facts/kms.md#kms-s3-sse-kms-put-get-permissions). The key policy already lets IAM policies control access, so one IAM statement is enough. Least privilege means you [specify the key ARN of each KMS key](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-least-privilege-key-arns) and add one action.
items.takeaway: With SSE-KMS, a download also needs kms:Decrypt on the key, and an upload needs kms:GenerateDataKey.
items.twin: If the stem said "only uploads new objects in single PUT requests" instead: allow kms:GenerateDataKey, because an upload needs [kms:GenerateDataKey permissions on the key](../facts/kms.md#kms-s3-sse-kms-put-get-permissions).
items.say: The bucket uses a KMS key, so the role also needs kms:Decrypt on that key to download.

solvers.stem_only: Downloading an SSE-KMS object makes S3 decrypt the data key on the caller's behalf, so the role needs kms:Decrypt on that one key ARN; the key policy already delegates to IAM, so an IAM statement is enough.

items.stem: A media company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances that creates large video files. Company policy requires that each file is encrypted at rest with a key that the security team controls in AWS KMS. The application must encrypt each file itself before it stores the file in Amazon S3. Later, other authorized applications must be able to decrypt each file. What should the application do for each file?

options.text: Call the Encrypt operation with the KMS key and the whole video file as the plaintext, and store the ciphertext that AWS KMS returns in Amazon S3.
options.why: The Encrypt operation takes plaintext of up to [4,096 bytes](../facts/kms.md#kms-encrypt-max-plaintext-4096-bytes), so a whole video file cannot go to AWS KMS directly.
options.misconception: sends a large file to the KMS Encrypt operation

options.text: Download the key material of the KMS key to the application, encrypt the file locally with that key material, and store the file in Amazon S3.
options.why: KMS keys [never leave the service unencrypted](../facts/kms.md#kms-keys-never-leave-unencrypted), so the application cannot download the key material of a KMS key.
options.misconception: believes the key material of a KMS key can be downloaded to an application

options.text: Call GenerateDataKey with the KMS key, encrypt the file locally with the plaintext data key, and store the encrypted data key with the encrypted file.
options.why: GenerateDataKey returns [a plaintext copy of the data key](../facts/kms.md#kms-generatedatakey-returns-plaintext-and-encrypted) for local encryption and an encrypted copy, which stays protected by the KMS key.

options.text: Call GenerateDataKey with the KMS key, encrypt the file locally with the plaintext data key, and store the plaintext data key with the encrypted file.
options.why: A plaintext data key beside the file lets anyone who reads the file decrypt it. AWS says to [safely store the encrypted data key](../facts/kms.md#kms-envelope-store-encrypted-data-key) with the data.
options.misconception: keeps the plaintext data key because the application needs it later

items.explanation: This pattern is envelope encryption. A KMS key protects a small data key, and the data key encrypts the large file outside AWS KMS. After use, the application should [remove it from memory as soon as possible](../facts/kms.md#kms-envelope-store-encrypted-data-key). Later, the encrypted data key can be [decrypted by only users with permissions](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-exported-data-key-encrypted-under-kms-key) to use the KMS key.
items.takeaway: Large data: call GenerateDataKey, encrypt locally, and store the encrypted data key with the data.
items.twin: If the stem said "short secrets of a few hundred bytes" instead: the Encrypt operation also works, because it encrypts plaintext of [up to 4,096 bytes](../facts/kms.md#kms-encrypt-max-plaintext-4096-bytes).
items.say: For big files I use envelope encryption: KMS gives a data key, and the app encrypts the file locally.

solvers.stem_only: Envelope encryption: call GenerateDataKey under the KMS key, encrypt the file locally with the plaintext data key, discard it, and store the encrypted data key next to the ciphertext; readers call kms:Decrypt on the encrypted data key.

items.stem: A company stores customer orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The table uses the default encryption at rest, and no one has changed its encryption settings. A new security rule says that the security team must decide which IAM roles can use the encryption key of the table. The team must also audit each use of that key in AWS CloudTrail. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: decide which IAM roles can use the encryption key
audit each use of that key

options.text: Switch the encryption of the table to the AWS managed key for DynamoDB, and edit the key policy of that key so that it names the allowed roles.
options.why: The service controls that key policy: you [cannot change any properties of AWS managed keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-managed-key-cannot-change), and the key policy is one of them.

options.text: Keep the AWS owned key that encrypts the table, and create an AWS CloudTrail trail that records each use of that key in the account.
options.why: For an AWS owned key, the logging of key use is [not viewable by the customer](../facts/kms.md#kms-key-type-logging-owned-not-viewable), so a new trail shows nothing about that key.
options.misconception: believes that the use of an AWS owned key appears in the company's own CloudTrail trail

options.text: Create a key in an AWS CloudHSM key store that the company operates, and switch the encryption of the table to that customer managed key.
options.why: A custom key store brings [additional cost, operational complexity, and reduced performance](../facts/kms.md#kms-custom-key-store-only-if-mandated), and no rule here asks for dedicated HSMs.
options.misconception: believes that control of a key needs hardware security modules that the company operates

options.text: Create a customer managed KMS key with a key policy that names the allowed roles, and switch the encryption of the table to that new key.
options.why: The key policy of a customer managed key is [exclusively controlled by the customer](../facts/kms.md#kms-key-type-key-policy-control), and its use goes to the [CloudTrail customer trail or event data store](../facts/kms.md#kms-key-type-logging-owned-not-viewable).

items.explanation: DynamoDB lets you [switch between these key types at any time](../facts/kms.md#kms-dynamodb-always-encrypted-three-key-types). AWS owned keys [do not provide policy controls or CloudTrail logs](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-aws-owned-no-policy-no-logs). With a customer managed key, [you have full control over these KMS keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-customer-managed-key-full-control), including the key policy, and the team reads each use in CloudTrail.
items.takeaway: Control of the key policy plus an audit trail of each use points to a customer managed key.
items.twin: If the stem said "must encrypt the data and needs no control or audit of the key" instead: keep the AWS owned key, because it fits unless you are [required to audit or control the encryption key](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-owned-key-good-choice-unless-audit).
items.say: If you must control and audit the key, use a customer managed key; the default AWS owned key gives you neither.

solvers.stem_only: Default DynamoDB encryption uses an AWS owned key, which the company cannot control or see in CloudTrail; create a customer managed KMS key whose key policy names the allowed roles and switch the table to it (its use is logged in CloudTrail).

items.stem: A company has two AWS accounts in an organization in AWS Organizations. Account A owns a customer managed AWS KMS key that encrypts files in an Amazon S3 bucket. An application in account B runs with an IAM role and must decrypt data that is encrypted under this key. The key policy names only principals in account A. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with LEAST privilege? (Select TWO.)
keywords: Account A owns a customer managed AWS KMS key

options.text: In account B, attach a service control policy (SCP) to the account that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the key in account A.
options.why: [An SCP never grants permissions](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-never-grants-permissions), so it cannot replace an allow in the IAM policy of the role in account B.

options.text: In account A, add a statement to the key policy that allows kms:Decrypt for the ARN of the IAM role of the application in account B.
options.why: Across accounts, use of a key requires [permission in the key policy](../facts/kms.md#kms-cross-account-key-policy-and-iam-policy), and this statement names one role and one action.

options.text: In account B, add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:Decrypt with the wildcard character as the resource, so every key matches.
options.why: It works together with the key policy statement, but it matches every key, and best practice is to [specify the key ARN of each KMS key](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-least-privilege-key-arns).

options.text: In account B, add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the customer managed key in account A.
options.why: Account B also needs [an IAM policy in the external user's account](../facts/kms.md#kms-cross-account-key-policy-and-iam-policy), and this statement names one key ARN and one action.

options.text: In account A, re-encrypt the files under the AWS managed key for Amazon S3, and share that AWS managed key with account B.
options.why: The service controls the key policy of that key, and you [cannot change any properties of AWS managed keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-managed-key-cannot-change), so account B cannot be added.

items.explanation: The key and the role are in different accounts. Cross-account use of a key requires [permission in the key policy](../facts/kms.md#kms-cross-account-key-policy-and-iam-policy) of the key in account A and [an IAM policy in the external user's account](../facts/kms.md#kms-cross-account-key-policy-and-iam-policy) in account B. Each statement names one action and one role or key.
items.takeaway: Cross-account KMS use needs two allows: the key policy in the key's account and an IAM policy in the caller's account.
items.twin: If the stem said "an application role in account A" instead: one key policy statement that names the role is enough, because the key policy is [the primary way to control access](../facts/kms.md#kms-key-policy-primary-exactly-one).
items.say: Across accounts, the key policy must allow the role, and the role's own policy must allow the key.

solvers.stem_only: Cross-account KMS use needs both sides: the key policy in account A must allow the account B role (or account), and the role's IAM policy in account B must allow kms:Decrypt on the specific key ARN in account A.

A new application role has an IAM policy that allows s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on the bucket and allows no KMS actions. The application only uploads new objects in single PUT requests. Every request from the application fails with an access denied error. Which change will fix the problem with LEAST privilege?
keywords: only uploads new objects in single PUT requests

options.text: Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the customer managed key that encrypts the bucket.

items.stem: A financial services company is moving a Java application to AWS. Regulations require that the application's encryption keys are generated and stored in single-tenant hardware security modules (HSMs) under the company's exclusive control. The application calls its cryptographic library through the Java Cryptography Extension (JCE) interface, and the company does not want to change this code. The keys must stay available if one Availability Zone fails. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: single-tenant hardware security modules (HSMs) under the company's exclusive control

options.text: Create customer managed keys in AWS KMS in the default key store, and allow the application role to use the keys in each key policy.
options.why: AWS KMS has [no native integration](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-no-native-openssl-jce-cng) with JCE, and compared with KMS, CloudHSM is the service that gives a [single-tenant HSM cluster](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-vs-kms-faq-single-tenant-vpc-exclusive).
options.misconception: treats the KMS default key store as single-tenant HSMs under the company's exclusive control

options.text: Run HSM appliances that the company owns in two of its data centers, and connect them to the VPC through AWS Direct Connect.
options.why: It works, but the company runs hardware and network links itself, and CloudHSM already gives [exclusive control over how your keys are used](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-vs-kms-faq-single-tenant-vpc-exclusive).
options.misconception: believes that exclusive control of keys needs HSM hardware that the company owns

options.text: Create an AWS CloudHSM cluster with two HSMs in two Availability Zones, and generate and use the keys through the CloudHSM client libraries.
options.why: CloudHSM gives a [single-tenant HSM cluster](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-vs-kms-faq-single-tenant-vpc-exclusive) in the company's VPC and supports [Java JCE](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-faq-standard-apis), so the code stays the same.

options.text: Use the AWS managed keys that AWS KMS creates for each service, and limit their use by editing the key policy of each managed key.
options.why: You [cannot change any properties of AWS managed keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-managed-key-cannot-change), so the company can neither edit their key policies nor control them exclusively.

items.explanation: Compared with AWS KMS, CloudHSM gives a [single-tenant HSM cluster](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-vs-kms-faq-single-tenant-vpc-exclusive) with [exclusive control over how your keys are used](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-vs-kms-faq-single-tenant-vpc-exclusive). Its libraries support [Java JCE](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-faq-standard-apis). With [at least two HSMs](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-faq-ha-automatic-two-azs) across two Availability Zones, high availability is automatic.
items.takeaway: Single-tenant HSMs under your exclusive control, or a PKCS #11 or JCE interface, point to AWS CloudHSM.
items.twin: If the stem said "hardware security modules (HSMs) validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 3" instead: a KMS customer managed key, because all KMS keys use HSMs validated under [FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3](../facts/kms.md#kms-hsm-fips-140-3-level-3).
items.say: Single-tenant HSMs under your own control and a JCE interface mean CloudHSM, with two HSMs in two zones.

solvers.stem_only: Single-tenant HSMs under exclusive customer control with a JCE interface means AWS CloudHSM: a cluster with at least two HSMs in different AZs, used through the CloudHSM JCE provider/client libraries.

items.stem: A security team created a customer managed AWS KMS key with a custom key policy. The key policy has one statement, which gives full access to the team's administrator role. Developer roles have IAM policies that allow kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the key, but their Decrypt calls fail with an access denied error. From now on, the team wants to centrally manage access to this key with IAM policies, as it does for other resources. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: IAM policies that allow kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the key
centrally manage access to this key with IAM policies

options.text: Create a KMS grant for each developer role that allows kms:Decrypt on the key, and create another grant for every new developer role.
options.why: It works, but [grants are often used for temporary permissions](../facts/kms.md#kms-grant-allow-only-one-key-temporary), and one grant per role is not central management with IAM.
options.misconception: uses one grant per principal where one key policy statement lets IAM policies work

options.text: Attach an IAM policy to the developer roles that allows every KMS action, kms:*, with the wildcard character as the resource of the statement.
options.why: Without permission from the key policy, [IAM policies that allow permissions have no effect](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-policy-allow-needs-key-policy), even with every action on every resource.

options.text: Add a statement to the key policy that allows access for the account principal, so that IAM policies in the account can allow use of the key.
options.why: A statement for the account principal lets the account [use IAM policies to delegate the permissions](../facts/kms.md#kms-account-principal-delegates-to-iam), so the existing developer policies start to work.

options.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the developer roles, so that the roles get full access to every resource in the account.
options.why: AdministratorAccess is an IAM policy too, and without the key policy, [IAM policies that allow permissions have no effect](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-policy-allow-needs-key-policy) on the key.

items.explanation: A KMS key policy [does not automatically give permission to the account](../facts/kms.md#kms-key-policy-no-automatic-account-permission), so the IAM allows of the developers are ignored. [The default key policy enables IAM policies](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-policy-allow-needs-key-policy) with a statement for the account principal. Adding that statement turns on IAM-based access, and the team then manages access in IAM.
items.takeaway: A KMS key ignores IAM allows until its key policy has the statement for the account principal.
items.twin: If the stem said "one developer role needs access for one day" instead: create a grant, because [grants are often used for temporary permissions](../facts/kms.md#kms-grant-allow-only-one-key-temporary).
items.say: The key policy has to let IAM in first: add the account principal statement, then the IAM policies work.

solvers.stem_only: IAM policies only take effect for a KMS key when the key policy allows the account principal (arn:aws:iam::account:root); add that statement to the key policy, and the existing IAM Decrypt permissions start working.

items.stem: A company stores many terabytes of objects in Amazon S3. The objects are encrypted with a symmetric customer managed AWS KMS key, and the security team wrote its own key policy for that key. A new company policy requires the company to rotate the key material every year. The security team must keep control of the key policy. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: symmetric customer managed AWS KMS key
rotate the key material every year

options.text: Create a new customer managed key every year, re-encrypt all objects in the bucket under the new key, and then schedule the old key for deletion.
options.why: It works, but KMS [keeps previous versions of keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-auto-rotation-no-reencrypt) to decrypt old data, so the yearly re-encryption of many terabytes is work that rotation does not need.

options.text: Enable automatic key rotation on the customer managed key, and keep the existing key policy and the key ID that the applications already use.
options.why: Automatic rotation [changes only the current key material](../facts/kms.md#kms-rotation-same-logical-key-transparent), so the key ID and the key policy that the team wrote stay the same.

options.text: Run a scheduled AWS Lambda function every year that copies each object onto itself, so that Amazon S3 encrypts every object under new data keys.
options.why: New data keys are not new KMS key material. Key rotation [changes only the current key material](../facts/kms.md#kms-rotation-same-logical-key-transparent) of the KMS key, and this function does not touch it.

options.text: Switch the encryption of the bucket to the AWS managed key for Amazon S3, because AWS rotates the key material of that key every year.
options.why: The key would rotate, but the team would lose its own key policy, because you [cannot change any properties of AWS managed keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-managed-key-cannot-change).

items.explanation: Automatic rotation is the built-in answer for a symmetric customer managed key. KMS [keeps previous versions of keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-auto-rotation-no-reencrypt) to decrypt old objects and encrypts new requests under the newest version. The key stays [the same logical resource](../facts/kms.md#kms-rotation-same-logical-key-transparent), so the key policy, the key ID and the applications stay as they are.
items.takeaway: A yearly rotation rule on a symmetric customer managed key: enable automatic rotation, and re-encrypt nothing.
items.twin: If the stem said "an asymmetric RSA key that signs documents" instead: create a new key and move the alias, because [automatic key rotation is not supported](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-asym-hmac-no-auto-rotation-alias) for asymmetric keys.
items.say: Turn on automatic rotation: KMS keeps the old key material, so you don't re-encrypt anything.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: a symmetric customer managed key, many terabytes in Amazon S3, new key material every year, and the security team keeps its own key policy.
Before I look at the options, I predict automatic key rotation, because AWS KMS can rotate the key material of a symmetric customer managed key and keep the same key.
I remove the AWS managed key, because the team cannot change its key policy. I remove the yearly copy of the objects, because new data keys do not give the KMS key new key material.

Between automatic rotation and a new key with a full re-encryption, the difference is the work; the stem says many terabytes and LEAST operational overhead, and KMS keeps the old key material to decrypt old objects, so nothing needs re-encryption.
Check: automatic rotation gives new key material every year, keeps the key policy and the key ID, and moves no data. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Turn on automatic key rotation for the symmetric customer managed key; KMS rotates the key material yearly by default, keeps old material to decrypt existing data, and the key ID, ARN and key policy stay the same, so no re-encryption is needed.

items.stem: An application encrypts data on the client side with a single-Region AWS KMS key in us-east-1. The application replicates the encrypted data to us-west-2 for disaster recovery. During an outage in us-east-1, an application role in us-west-2 must decrypt the replicated data without a cross-Region call to us-east-1. The company accepts a one-time re-encryption of the existing data. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: without a cross-Region call to us-east-1

options.text: Update the existing single-Region key in us-east-1 so that it becomes a multi-Region key, and create a replica of that key in us-west-2.
options.why: The multi-Region property is fixed when a key is created: [you cannot convert a single-Region key](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-cannot-convert) to a multi-Region key.

options.text: Allow the application role in us-west-2 to use kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the existing key in us-east-1, and call that ARN during the outage.
options.why: A single-Region key is [stored and used only in the Region](../facts/kms.md#kms-single-region-key-stays-in-region) where it was created, so each decryption calls us-east-1 and fails in the outage.

options.text: Create a new multi-Region primary key in us-east-1, create a replica of it in us-west-2, and encrypt the data under the primary key.
options.why: Related multi-Region keys share [the same key material and key ID](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-same-material-no-cross-region-call), so the replica in us-west-2 decrypts the data with no call to us-east-1.

options.text: Create a single-Region key in us-west-2, and run a scheduled job that decrypts each replicated object and re-encrypts it under that key.
options.why: It works for objects that the job already handled, but it is a job to run, and related multi-Region keys decrypt [without re-encrypting or making a cross-Region call](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-same-material-no-cross-region-call).
options.misconception: believes that data must be re-encrypted in each Region where it is read

options.text: Write a key policy for the replica key in us-west-2 that allows the application role in us-west-2 to use the replica key for decryption.
options.why: Each related key keeps its own policy, because you [manage each multi-Region key independently](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-independent-policies-grants-aliases), so the replica needs a statement for the role.

items.explanation: The recovery Region needs its own key for the data. Related multi-Region keys have [the same key material and key ID](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-same-material-no-cross-region-call), so a replica decrypts locally. You [manage each multi-Region key independently](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-independent-policies-grants-aliases), so the replica gets its own key policy for the role.
items.takeaway: Decrypt in a second Region with no cross-Region call: a multi-Region key with a replica that has its own key policy.
items.twin: If the stem said "data in each Region must be decryptable in that Region alone" instead: use single-Region keys, because with them keys in a Region can [decrypt sensitive data only in that Region](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-data-residency-harder).
items.say: Use a multi-Region key: the replica has the same key material, so the recovery Region decrypts on its own.

solvers.stem_only: A single-Region key cannot be converted to a multi-Region key, so create a new multi-Region primary key in us-east-1, replicate it to us-west-2, re-encrypt the data under it, and give the replica its own key policy that allows the us-west-2 role to decrypt locally.

items.stem: A company encrypts the data of one customer with a dedicated customer managed AWS KMS key. The contract with that customer ends today. The company must stop every cryptographic use of the key as soon as possible. A legal review in 60 days can require the company to read the data again, so the company must make sure that access can be restored. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: stop every cryptographic use of the key as soon as possible
make sure that access can be restored

options.text: Schedule the key for deletion with the longest waiting period, and cancel the deletion if the legal review requires access to the data.
options.why: The waiting period is [7 – 30 days](../facts/kms.md#kms-deletion-waiting-period-7-to-30-days), shorter than the review, and after deletion [that data becomes unrecoverable](../facts/kms.md#kms-deletion-irreversible-data-unrecoverable).

options.text: Remove kms:Decrypt and kms:Encrypt from every IAM policy in the account that names the key, and keep the key policy as it is.
options.why: The key policy is [the primary way to control access](../facts/kms.md#kms-key-policy-primary-exactly-one), and it can still allow principals directly, so IAM changes do not stop every use.

options.text: Add a statement to the key policy that denies all cryptographic operations to every principal, and remove that statement after the legal review.
options.why: It works, but the policy edits are extra work: a disabled key is blocked from cryptographic use [until you re-enable it](../facts/kms.md#kms-disabled-key-no-crypto-until-reenabled).
options.misconception: writes a deny statement for what one key state already does

options.text: Disable the key now, and enable the key again later if the legal review requires the company to read the data of the customer.
options.why: A disabled key cannot be used in any cryptographic operation [until you re-enable it](../facts/kms.md#kms-disabled-key-no-crypto-until-reenabled), so enabling it again restores access.

items.explanation: Disabling is the reversible switch. AWS suggests [disabling the KMS key instead of deleting it](../facts/kms.md#kms-disable-instead-of-delete) when you are not sure that you no longer need it. A disabled key cannot be used [until you re-enable it](../facts/kms.md#kms-disabled-key-no-crypto-until-reenabled), and enabling it again brings back access to the data.
items.takeaway: Stop key use with a way back: disable the key. Schedule deletion for data that the company will not read again.
items.twin: If the stem said "the data must become unreadable for good" instead: schedule the key for deletion, because after deletion [that data becomes unrecoverable](../facts/kms.md#kms-deletion-irreversible-data-unrecoverable).
items.say: Disable the key: nothing can use it, and you can enable it again after the legal review.

solvers.stem_only: Disable the KMS key: it immediately blocks all cryptographic operations and can be re-enabled at any time; scheduling deletion is wrong because the maximum waiting period (30 days) is shorter than 60 days.

items.stem: A company signs contracts with an asymmetric RSA key in AWS KMS. Customers verify the signatures with the public key of that KMS key. The applications that sign contracts refer to the key through an alias, not through its key ID. A new security policy requires the company to rotate the signing key. The applications must keep working without code changes. What should the company do?

options.text: Create a new asymmetric RSA KMS key for signing, and update the alias so that it points to the new KMS key instead of the old one.
options.why: Asymmetric keys rotate by hand: a new KMS key, then [mapping an existing key alias](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-asym-hmac-no-auto-rotation-alias) to it, so the applications keep the same alias.

options.text: Enable automatic key rotation on the existing asymmetric KMS key, and keep the alias that points to the existing KMS key.
options.why: Asymmetric KMS keys are [not eligible for automatic or on-demand key rotation](../facts/kms.md#kms-rotation-not-for-asymmetric-hmac-custom-store), so this setting does not exist for the key.
options.misconception: believes that automatic rotation works for every KMS key type

options.text: Start an on-demand rotation of the existing asymmetric KMS key, and keep the alias that points to the existing KMS key.
options.why: On-demand rotation is a feature of symmetric keys, and asymmetric KMS keys are [not eligible for automatic or on-demand key rotation](../facts/kms.md#kms-rotation-not-for-asymmetric-hmac-custom-store).
options.misconception: believes that on-demand rotation covers asymmetric keys

options.text: Import new RSA key material into the existing asymmetric KMS key, and keep the alias that points to the existing KMS key.
options.why: An asymmetric key with imported material is [permanently associated with that key material](../facts/kms.md#kms-imported-asym-hmac-same-material-only), so different material cannot replace it.
options.misconception: believes that new key material can replace the material of an asymmetric KMS key

items.explanation: [Automatic key rotation is not supported](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-asym-hmac-no-auto-rotation-alias) for asymmetric KMS keys, so the company rotates by hand. Manual rotation means a new KMS key. Without an alias, you must [update references to the KMS key ID](../facts/kms.md#kms-manual-rotation-new-key-alias); with an alias, the applications need no change.
items.takeaway: To rotate an asymmetric or HMAC key, create a new KMS key and move the alias to it.
items.twin: If the stem said "a symmetric encryption KMS key" instead: enable automatic key rotation, because for a customer managed key [automatic rotation is optional](../facts/kms.md#kms-rotation-only-customer-managed-symmetric).
items.say: Asymmetric keys don't rotate automatically, so create a new key and point the alias at it.

solvers.stem_only: Asymmetric KMS keys support neither automatic nor on-demand rotation, so rotate manually: create a new asymmetric RSA signing key and repoint the alias the applications use to the new key (customers get the new public key).

items.stem: A financial services company is moving a Java application to AWS. Regulations require that the application's encryption keys are protected by hardware security modules (HSMs) validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 3. The application calls AWS KMS through the AWS SDK. The security team must write the key policy of each key and must not depend on keys that an AWS service controls. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: hardware security modules (HSMs) validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 3
must write the key policy of each key

options.text: Create customer managed keys in AWS KMS in the default key store, and allow the application role to use the keys in each key policy.
options.why: All AWS KMS keys are protected by HSMs validated under [FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3](../facts/kms.md#kms-change-hsm-fips-140-2-level-3-2023-05), and the security team writes the key policy of a customer managed key.

options.text: Run HSM appliances that the company owns in two of its data centers, and connect them to the VPC through AWS Direct Connect.
options.why: It adds hardware and network links to run, and the keys in AWS KMS already use HSMs validated under [FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3](../facts/kms.md#kms-hsm-fips-140-3-level-3).

options.text: Create an AWS CloudHSM cluster with two HSMs in two Availability Zones, and generate and use the keys through the CloudHSM client libraries.
options.why: It works, but the company operates the HSMs, and AWS suggests AWS KMS when you do not want to [operate your own HSMs](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-consider-kms-if-no-hsm-ops).

options.text: Use the AWS managed keys that AWS KMS creates for each service, and limit their use by editing the key policy of each managed key.
options.why: You [cannot change any properties of AWS managed keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-managed-key-cannot-change), so the security team cannot write their key policies.

items.explanation: AWS KMS meets this mandate without extra hardware: today all AWS KMS keys are protected by HSMs validated under [FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3](../facts/kms.md#kms-change-hsm-fips-140-2-level-3-2023-05). AWS recommends customer managed keys [created and stored in the KMS HSMs](../facts/kms.md#kms-recommend-cmk-in-kms-hsms), and their key policy is [exclusively controlled by the customer](../facts/kms.md#kms-key-type-key-policy-control).
items.takeaway: A FIPS level mandate alone does not call for CloudHSM: all KMS keys use HSMs validated under [FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3](../facts/kms.md#kms-hsm-fips-140-3-level-3).
items.twin: If the stem said "single-tenant hardware security modules (HSMs) under the company's exclusive control" instead: a CloudHSM cluster, because CloudHSM gives a [single-tenant HSM cluster](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-vs-kms-faq-single-tenant-vpc-exclusive).
items.say: KMS keys already sit in FIPS Level 3 HSMs, so a customer managed key meets the rule without CloudHSM.

solvers.stem_only: AWS KMS HSMs are validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 3, so customer managed keys in the default KMS key store meet the requirement, keep the SDK code unchanged, and let the security team write each key policy, with far less overhead than CloudHSM.

verification.note: swapped out of the shipped set: stem names AWS KMS (exam-011), twin differs in several phrases (exam-010), difficulty mix (exam-009)
